title: How do you make pretty and consistent 2D sprites?
author: Fr3yz
selftext:
Title, mostly 32x32 to 64x64 for topdown RPG. I mainly use Opus 5.5 and sometimes it does create pretty or consistent sprites. But being consistent and pretty is a difficult ideal to aim when it scales.

I've tried using reference images, but it's not perfect yet. I don't know how to scale this up and make 20+ sprites based on like 3-4 templates. This includes idle animations, walking and attacking which adds complexity. I don't know if MCP is even necessary.

What's your workflow?

comments.author: YannLeCoomer
comments.body:
Alright I can't sleep so I got on my computer lol, and believe me, I got you. Before I went up to 96x96 I had a 64x64 sprite (ChatGPT is saying this one is 52px tall at its tallest) that was cute and looks like some of the other stuff you posted in this thread. 64x64 was way way easier to produce than 96x96 but I really like the new character design and anyway I'll just paste in my process. You can definitely develop your process with Opus and honestly once you've got what you want down you can probably use Haiku to hit the PixelLab API. Anyway, incoming wall of text:

PixelLab's API accessed through ChatGPT (though Claude would work fine here too). Basically make your concept art with your favorite image generator, then draft what your ideal pixel character looks like (I find the big AI players understand intent a bit better and you can draft something easier this way than going straight to a specialized AI tool like PixelLab).

Once you've got something that isn't actually pixel art but looks kinda like it, you load it into PixelLab and say "the correct output will look like this reference image". You can do the same thing with all 8 directions at once, and in fact should because the more context you can feed the image generator of your character viewed from different angles, the more things will be consistent between directions.

You then have some candidates for each direction, keep generating and iterating with your AI until you have an approved idle frame for each direction. Then tell your AI that there should be a max 32-color pallet for the character and it'll do some algorithm to get each one down to the same 32-color set (this vastly improves color consistency during animation and is what I learned after I generated my main character's animations and I'm not going to go back lol)

Then load them all up in Pixen or something and fix the stray pixels and weird sharpness, correct eye color etc.

Then you have your character with an idle state. You basically go through this process for each animation you'd like as well. e.g. Generate a walking frame, iterate till you like them all, 32 color reduction, clean them up, then use PixMiniMax to generate the animation. Once you like all the animations you need to go over every single frame in Pixen to remove stray pixels and the like which really makes a huge difference for the end product.

If you want good results it will require manual effort.

https://i.redd.it/5bklplcactth1.gif

replies.author: YannLeCoomer
replies.body:
I use the API, and you want to create a daily task for your AI to check the MCP and API routes because they change frequently. API has historically had more capabilities than MCP but that might change. Point your Claude here: [https://api.pixellab.ai/v2/openapi.json](https://api.pixellab.ai/v2/openapi.json) and I guess just tell it to find the MCP docs too lol

I am actually lowkey convinced the API is not accurately measured. I've been generating a metric assload of sprite and animation frames. I had my ChatGPT estimate it recently and it said 5,000 frames were generated this month, and I'm at 3000/5000 used tokens. I know this sounds like an ad, but with the $20 plan you can generate a metric fuckton of sprites.

The lower res ones I'm attaching are older and done in the web UI, but the API with your chatbot will always be better, you have so much more control.

https://i.redd.it/p41kv6hdetth1.gif
